mn115:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
mn115:1.3: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:
mn115:2.1: “Bhikkhus, whatever fears arise, all arise because of the fool, not because of the wise man;
mn115:2.2: whatever perils arise, all arise because of the fool, not because of the wise man;
mn115:2.3: whatever calamities arise, all arise because of the fool, not because of the wise man.
mn115:2.4: Just as, bhikkhus, a fire that starts in a reed hut or a grass hut burns down even a gabled house, plastered inside and out, draught-proof, with bolted doors and shuttered windows,
mn115:2.5: so too, bhikkhus, whatever fears arise, all arise because of the fool, not because of the wise man;
mn115:2.6: whatever perils arise, all arise because of the fool, not because of the wise man;
mn115:2.7: whatever calamities arise, all arise because of the fool, not because of the wise man.
mn115:2.8: So, bhikkhus, the fool brings fear, the wise man is free from fear;
mn115:2.9: the fool brings peril, the wise man is free from peril;
mn115:2.10: the fool brings calamity, the wise man is free from calamity.
mn115:2.11: There is no fear from the wise man, bhikkhus, there is no peril from the wise man, there is no calamity from the wise man.
mn115:2.12: Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train thus: ‘We shall be wise men and inquirers’—
mn115:2.13: that is how you should train yourselves.”[^1]
mn115:3.1: When this was said, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
mn115:3.2: “In what way, venerable sir, is a wise bhikkhu worthy to be called an inquirer?”
mn115:3.3: “When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is skilled in the elements, skilled in the bases, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in the possible and the impossible—
mn115:3.4: in this way, Ānanda, a wise bhikkhu is worthy to be called an inquirer.”
mn115:4.1: “But, venerable sir, in what way is a bhikkhu worthy to be called skilled in the elements?”
mn115:4.3: the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element;
mn115:4.4: the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element;
mn115:4.5: the nose element, the odour element, the nose-consciousness element;
mn115:4.6: the tongue element, the flavour element, the tongue-consciousness element;
mn115:4.7: the body element, the tangible element, the body-consciousness element;
mn115:4.8: the mind element, the dhamma element, the mind-consciousness element.
mn115:4.9: When, Ānanda, he knows and sees these eighteen elements—
mn115:4.10: in this way too, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements.”
mn115:5.1: “But, venerable sir, might there be another way in which a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements?”
mn115:5.3: There are, Ānanda, these six elements:
mn115:5.4: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, the consciousness element.
mn115:5.5: When, Ānanda, he knows and sees these six elements—
mn115:5.6: in this way too, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements.”
mn115:6.1: “But, venerable sir, might there be another way in which a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements?”
mn115:6.3: There are, Ānanda, these six elements:
mn115:6.4: the pleasure element, the pain element, the joy element, the grief element, the equanimity element, the ignorance element.
mn115:6.5: When, Ānanda, he knows and sees these six elements—
mn115:6.6: in this way too, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements.”
mn115:7.1: “But, venerable sir, might there be another way in which a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements?”
mn115:7.3: There are, Ānanda, these six elements:
mn115:7.4: the sensual-desire element, the renunciation element, the ill-will element, the non-ill-will element, the cruelty element, the non-cruelty element.
mn115:7.5: When, Ānanda, he knows and sees these six elements—
mn115:7.6: in this way too, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements.”
mn115:8.1: “But, venerable sir, might there be another way in which a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements?”
mn115:8.3: There are, Ānanda, these three elements:
mn115:8.4: the sensual-desire element, the form element, the formless element.
mn115:8.5: When, Ānanda, he knows and sees these three elements—
mn115:8.6: in this way too, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements.”
mn115:9.1: “But, venerable sir, might there be another way in which a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements?”
mn115:9.3: There are, Ānanda, these two elements:
mn115:9.4: the conditioned element, the unconditioned element.
mn115:9.5: When, Ānanda, he knows and sees these two elements—
mn115:9.6: in this way too, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements.”
mn115:10.1: “But, venerable sir, in what way is a bhikkhu worthy to be called skilled in the bases?”
mn115:10.2: “There are, Ānanda, these six internal and external bases:
mn115:10.3: the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odours, the tongue and flavours, the body and tangibles, the mind and dhammas.
mn115:10.4: When, Ānanda, he knows and sees these six internal and external bases—
mn115:10.5: in this way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the bases.”
mn115:11.1: “But, venerable sir, in what way is a bhikkhu worthy to be called skilled in dependent origination?”
mn115:11.3: ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.
mn115:11.4: When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases; that is to say:
mn115:11.8: with name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base;
mn115:11.9: with the sixfold base as condition, contact;
mn115:11.15: with birth as condition, ageing and death come to be, and also sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief and despair.
mn115:11.16: That is how there is an origin to this whole mass of suffering.
mn115:11.17: But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, cessation of formations;
mn115:11.18: with the cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness;
mn115:11.19: with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form;
mn115:11.20: with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the sixfold base;
mn115:11.21: with the cessation of the sixfold base, cessation of contact;
mn115:11.22: with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling;
mn115:11.23: with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving;
mn115:11.24: with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging;
mn115:11.25: with the cessation of clinging, cessation of being;
mn115:11.26: with the cessation of being, cessation of birth;
mn115:11.27: with the cessation of birth, ageing and death cease, and also sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief and despair.
mn115:11.28: That is how there is a cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’
mn115:11.29: In this way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in dependent origination.”
mn115:12.1: “But, venerable sir, in what way is a bhikkhu worthy to be called skilled in the possible and the impossible?”
mn115:12.2: “Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu understands: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view could treat any formation as permanent—no such possibility exists’;
mn115:12.3: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an ordinary person could treat some formation as permanent—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:12.4: He understands: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view could treat any formation as pleasurable—no such possibility exists’;
mn115:12.5: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an ordinary person could treat some formation as pleasurable—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:12.6: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view could treat any dhamma as self—no such possibility exists’, he understands;[^2]
mn115:12.7: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an ordinary person could treat some dhamma as self—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:13.1: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view could deprive his mother of life—no such possibility exists’, he understands;
mn115:13.2: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an ordinary person could deprive his mother of life—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:13.3: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view could deprive his father of life …
mn115:13.4: could deprive an Arahant of life—such a possibility exists’, he understands;
mn115:13.5: ‘it is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view could, with a mind of hate, shed a Tathāgata’s blood—no such possibility exists’, he understands;
mn115:13.6: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an ordinary person could, with a mind of hate, shed a Tathāgata’s blood—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:13.7: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view could cause a schism in the Saṅgha—no such possibility exists’, he understands;
mn115:13.8: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an ordinary person could cause a schism in the Saṅgha—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:13.9: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view could acknowledge another teacher—no such possibility exists’, he understands;[^3]
mn115:13.10: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an ordinary person could acknowledge another teacher—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:14.1: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that two Arahants, Fully Enlightened Ones, could arise contemporaneously in one world-system—no such possibility exists’, he understands;[^4]
mn115:14.2: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a single Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, could arise in one world-system—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:14.3: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that two Wheel-turning Monarchs could arise contemporaneously in one world-system—no such possibility exists’, he understands;
mn115:14.4: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a single Wheel-turning Monarch could arise in one world-system—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:15.1: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a woman could be an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One—no such possibility exists’, he understands;[^5]
mn115:15.2: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a man could be an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:15.3: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a woman could be a Wheel-turning Monarch—no such possibility exists’, he understands;
mn115:15.4: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a man could be a Wheel-turning Monarch—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:15.5: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a woman could occupy the status of Sakka … the status of Māra … the status of a Brahmā—no such possibility exists’, he understands;
mn115:15.6: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a man could occupy the status of Sakka … the status of Māra … the status of a Brahmā—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:16.1: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a wished-for, desired, agreeable result could come from bad bodily conduct—no such possibility exists’, he understands;
mn115:16.2: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an unwished-for, undesired, disagreeable result could come from bad bodily conduct—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:16.3: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a wished-for, desired, agreeable result could come from bad verbal conduct …
mn115:16.4: from bad mental conduct—no such possibility exists’, he understands;
mn115:16.5: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an unwished-for, undesired, disagreeable result could come from bad verbal conduct …
mn115:16.6: from bad mental conduct—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:17.1: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that an unwished-for, undesired, disagreeable result could come from good bodily conduct—no such possibility exists’, he understands;
mn115:17.2: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a wished-for, desired, agreeable result could come from good bodily conduct—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:17.3: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that an unwished-for, undesired, disagreeable result could come from good verbal conduct …
mn115:17.4: from good mental conduct—no such possibility exists’, he understands;
mn115:17.5: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a wished-for, desired, agreeable result could come from good verbal conduct …
mn115:17.6: from good mental conduct—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:18.1: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person possessed of bad bodily conduct could, because of that, for that reason,[^6] on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in the heavenly world—no such possibility exists’, he understands;
mn115:18.2: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a person possessed of bad bodily conduct could, because of that, for that reason, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:19.1: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person possessed of bad verbal conduct …
mn115:19.2: possessed of bad mental conduct could, because of that, for that reason, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in the heavenly world—no such possibility exists’, he understands;
mn115:19.3: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a person possessed of bad verbal conduct …
mn115:19.4: possessed of bad mental conduct could, because of that, for that reason, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:19.5: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person possessed of good bodily conduct could, because of that, for that reason, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell—no such possibility exists’, he understands;
mn115:19.6: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a person possessed of good bodily conduct could, because of that, for that reason, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in the heavenly world—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:19.7: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person possessed of good verbal conduct …
mn115:19.8: possessed of good mental conduct could, because of that, for that reason, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell—no such possibility exists’, he understands;
mn115:19.9: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a person possessed of good verbal conduct …
mn115:19.10: possessed of good mental conduct could, because of that, for that reason, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in the heavenly world—such a possibility exists.’
mn115:19.11: In this way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the possible and the impossible.”
mn115:20.1: When this was said, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
mn115:20.2: “It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvellous.
mn115:20.3: What is the name of this discourse on the Dhamma, venerable sir?”
mn115:20.4: “Therefore, Ānanda, you may remember this discourse on the Dhamma as ‘The Many Kinds of Elements’, and also as ‘The Four Cycles’, and also as ‘The Mirror of the Dhamma’, and also as ‘The Drum of the Deathless’, and also as ‘The Unsurpassed Victory in Battle.’”
mn115:20.5: This is what the Blessed One said.
mn115:20.6: The venerable Ānanda was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
